title: Reading Food Web Diagrams
keyIdea: A food web is many food chains joined together. Each arrow points from the food to the eater. Every chain starts with a producer, a plant that makes food from sunlight. Primary consumers eat plants, and secondary consumers eat other animals. Decomposers such as fungi break down dead things into nutrients for the soil. Because the chains are linked, removing one species changes the numbers of what it ate and of what ate it.
familyTip: Pick an animal you saw today, such as a blackbird, and list what it eats and what might eat it. Draw arrows from food to eater, then ask: if one of those disappeared, who would go hungry and who would do well?

visual.caption: Producer or consumer? Drag each card into a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find every eater of the mouse, label producers and consumers, trace two chains, take frogs and rabbits away, and recycle a dead hawk.

kid: A food web shows who eats what in a place. It is lots of food chains joined up. Each arrow points from the food to the eater. So mouse → snake means the snake eats the mouse.
Every chain starts with a producer. A producer is a plant. It makes its own food from sunlight. Animals that eat plants are primary consumers. Animals that eat other animals are secondary consumers.
To read a web, start at a plant and follow the arrows up. In a meadow, grass → grasshopper → frog → hawk is one chain. Berries → mouse → hawk is another. The hawk is in both.

Living things in a web depend on each other. If the frogs vanished, grasshoppers would go up, because nothing would eat them. Snakes and hawks would eat more mice. Decomposers, like fungi, break down dead plants and animals into food for the soil.
adult: Ages 8 to 9. This matches Year 4 Living things and their habitats in the National Curriculum in England (construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey; recognise that environments can change and that this can pose dangers to living things) and NGSS 5-LS2-1 (model the movement of matter among plants, animals, decomposers and the environment). It builds on Simple Food Chains.

A food web links the food chains in one habitat. Arrows show the direction food and energy move, from the organism eaten to the one that eats it. Producers make their own food by photosynthesis. Primary consumers eat producers, and secondary consumers eat other consumers. Decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil, which plants then take up.

Common mistakes: reading arrows the wrong way, as 'eats' instead of 'is eaten by'. Calling an animal a producer because other animals feed on it. Deciding a role from size rather than diet. Thinking a predator dies out if one prey vanishes, when a web gives it other foods. And leaving decomposers out of the picture.

In the lab your child finds every animal that eats the mouse and gives six living things their role. They build two chains that end at the hawk and spot what the chains share. They take the frogs away, then the rabbits, and follow the effects along the arrows. Last, they pass a dead hawk to the fungi and send the nutrients back to the plants.

practice.prompt: In a food web, an arrow goes from the grasshopper to the frog. What does it show?
practice.hint: Arrows point from the food to the eater.
practice.explain: The arrow points to the eater, so the frog eats the grasshopper. Food and energy move from the grasshopper to the frog.

practice.prompt: Frogs eat grasshoppers. In a food web, a frog is a…
practice.hint: Does the frog eat plants or animals?
practice.explain: A frog eats an animal, the grasshopper, so it is a secondary consumer. Primary consumers eat plants; producers are plants.

practice.prompt: A snake eats {a} frogs and {b} mice each month. All the frogs disappear. If the snake still needs the same number of meals, how many mice must it eat each month?
practice.hint: Its frog meals must be replaced by mouse meals.
practice.explain: It needs {=a+b} meals: {a} that were frogs plus {b} mice. So it eats {=a+b} mice, and the mice are hit too. That is how a change spreads through a web.

practice.prompt: In a web, {a} different plants are each eaten by rabbits, and rabbits are eaten by foxes. Nothing else is in the web. How many food chains end at the fox?
practice.hint: Each plant starts its own chain: plant → rabbit → fox.
practice.explain: Each of the {a} plants starts one chain to the fox, so there are {a} chains. A web is many chains joined.

practice.prompt: Only frogs eat grasshoppers in a meadow. If all the frogs went, what would happen to the grasshoppers?
practice.explain: With nothing eating them, more grasshoppers survive, so their numbers go up. They might then eat more grass.

pool.prompt: Every food chain in a food web starts with…
pool.explain: Chains start with a producer, a plant that makes its own food. Energy then passes to the animals that eat it.

pool.prompt: Foxes eat rabbits and mice. If the rabbits vanished, what would most likely happen?
choices: all the foxes would die at once
pool.hint: Does the fox have another food in the web?
pool.explain: The fox still has mice, so it eats more of them. The mice may then fall in number too.

pool.prompt: A deer eats only grass and leaves, but it is big. It is a…
pool.hint: The role depends on what it eats, not how big it is.
pool.explain: It eats only plants, so it is a primary consumer, whatever its size.

pool.prompt: What do decomposers such as fungi and worms do?
choices: break down dead things into nutrients for the soil
pool.hint: Think about what happens to a fallen leaf or a dead animal.
pool.explain: Decomposers break down dead plants and animals. The nutrients go into the soil, and plants take them up.

pool.prompt: An owl eats {a} mice and {b} voles each week. The voles disappear. If the owl still needs the same number of meals, how many mice must it eat each week?
pool.hint: Every vole meal must become a mouse meal.
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b}. The owl now eats {=a+b} mice a week, so losing voles puts more pressure on the mice.

pool.prompt: A pond web has {a} kinds of water plant. Each is eaten by tadpoles, and a heron eats the tadpoles. Nothing else is in the web. How many food chains end at the heron?
pool.hint: Count one chain for each producer.
pool.explain: Each plant starts a chain: plant → tadpole → heron. That gives {a} chains ending at the heron.

pool.prompt: In a web, grass → grasshopper → frog → hawk and berries → mouse → hawk are two chains. Which living thing is in both?
pool.hint: Look for a name that appears in each chain.
pool.explain: The hawk ends both chains. Shared species are what join chains into a web.

pool.prompt: Sam says grass is a consumer because rabbits eat it. What is wrong?
choices: grass makes its own food, so it is a producer
pool.hint: Does grass eat anything, or make its own food?
pool.explain: Being eaten does not make something a consumer. Grass makes its own food from sunlight, so it is a producer.
